summary: Describes a sub-delegation of the ietf URN namespace for registered protocol parameters. The ietf namespace from RFC 2648 gives lasting names to IETF-defined things, and this adds a branch for registered items. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo gives parameters a permanent name in a big naming tree. It adds a new branch under an existing branch.

questions: what is the ietf urn namespace
how do i register an iana parameter as a urn
subtitle: Gives IANA-registered protocol parameters stable URN names under urn:ietf:params.

tldr.problem: Standards often need to refer to registered protocol items as URIs, and doing that in an ad hoc way had led to interoperability problems.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC creates a sub-delegation called params below the ietf URN namespace, and sets a template that a registry fills in, put in the IANA considerations section of the specifying document.
tldr.outcome: Registered items get names that never change meaning, such as urn:ietf:params:dns:rr-type-codes:soa, though no resolution mechanism is defined.

facts.label: Template fields
facts.value: 4: Registry name, Specification, Repository, Index value

today: RFC 3553 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 73) and no RFC obsoleting or updating it is listed in the unit metadata.

sections.title: Why Registered Items Need URNs
sections.content:
IETF standards often require registering protocol elements in a central repository. The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) keeps that repository and takes direction from the IETF. It holds lists such as assigned port numbers, MIME media types and enterprise numbers.

Over time a need arose to refer to these items as URIs. The RFC says this was done in an ad hoc way that easily caused interoperability problems. It creates a sub-delegation called params below the ietf URN namespace, which is defined in RFC 2648, as a standard way to name items registered for IETF standards. Assignments below it are specified in an RFC through the IETF consensus process and include the template of Section 4.
sections.plainLanguage: Many official lists of numbers and names exist, but people wrote down links to them in messy, different ways. This memo gives them one tidy way to write the address.

sections.title: How the params Names Are Structured
sections.content:
The registrant of the sub-namespace is the Internet Engineering Task Force. The namespace is primarily opaque. IANA may take suggestions for names but reserves the right to assign whatever name it wants, within guidelines set by the IESG.

A colon denotes a very limited hierarchy. If a name contains a colon, both sides are valid names, and the left side generally names a class of items that contains the others. The RFC's example: a name can be assigned to the whole list of DNS resource record type codes and to each individual code.

Lexical equivalence is an exact string match under the URN syntax rules of RFC 2141. No additional characters are reserved, there is no validation mechanism, and the scope is global.
sections.plainLanguage: Most names are just labels the librarian picks. A colon works like a folder: the part before it is the big group, and the part after is one thing inside it.

sections.title: Uniqueness and Persistence
sections.content:
The IESG uses the IETF consensus process to make sure sub-namespaces produce unique names. It delegates to IANA the job of keeping the sub-namespace names unique, by comparing a new name with the list of earlier ones. If there is a conflict, IANA asks the registrant for a new string until it is resolved.

Persistence is strict: once a name has been allocated it MUST NOT be re-allocated for a different purpose, and the assignment rules MUST ensure that the meaning of values cannot change. The mechanism is not appropriate for values that change over time. In that case the name MUST identify the container or concept, not the value. The RFC's example is that urn:ietf:params:foo-params:foo may name a slot, while naming the changing value itself is only valid for something persistent and unique such as a version number.

Identifiers are assigned only after the item has been registered with IANA using standard procedures, or documented in an RFC describing a standards track protocol. At this time no resolution mechanism is defined.
sections.plainLanguage: Once an address is given out it belongs to that thing forever. If something keeps changing, the address points at the box that holds it, not the changing thing.

sections.title: Assigning Names with the Template
sections.content:
For most flat registries the required elements are small: the registry name, a reference to the relevant documents, a statement of which repositories hold the authoritative data, and a statement of which element is the value used in the URN, usually the index value assigned by IANA. More complex registries, such as DNS parameters, repeat this for sub-namespaces and should say whether a name for the sub-namespace itself is valid.

The template has four fields:

  • Registry name: the name of the sub-namespace, often the same as IANA's name for the registry.
  • Specification: the IETF documents defining the registry and its items.
  • Repository: where the registry currently lives. It will change over time and is only a hint for the initial mapping.
  • Index value: how a registered value is embedded in the URI. It MUST detail any transformations needed to meet URN syntax and any canonicalization so that case-sensitive comparison gives the expected equivalences.

To request a name, put the template, or a reference to it, in the IANA considerations section of the specifying document.
sections.plainLanguage: To get an address you fill in a short form: what the list is called, which document describes it, where it lives, and how each entry is written in the address.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC lists none beyond those already inherent to using URNs. General URN considerations are in RFC 2141, and further ones for one particular URN resolution method are in RFC 3404, part of the series that starts with RFC 3401.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new is risky here. The usual cautions for these kinds of addresses still apply.

sections.title: The Burden on IANA
sections.content:
The RFC admits it puts a new and significant burden on IANA, since each new IANA registry may need an additional assignment process. To reduce that burden, any parameter namespace registration must be very clear about its criteria for inclusion.

It also argues a benefit: defining a registry that fits the constraints of a URN namespace imposes extra discipline that should take some of the guess-work out of creating and maintaining the registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The list keepers get more work, so each request has to be very clear. The tidy rules should also make the lists easier to look after.
